title: Owo Soup
author: Dobby Eghosa
desc: Thickened with both sieved garri and starch, and made creamy yellow by a teaspoon of pounded native salt emulsifying the palm oil off the heat before it goes in.
longDesc: Owo is the creamy yellow soup of the Urhobo, Itsekiri and Isoko, and the technique that makes it is an emulsification. Three handfuls of sieved yellow garri thicken a litre and a half of water into a base; separately, a teaspoon of pounded native salt is mixed with two handfuls of starch, two cooking spoons of palm oil and a cup of water until it flows freely, and that mixture is what turns the soup yellow and creamy rather than letting the oil sit separate. Note the constraint on crayfish: only a teaspoon, because too much turns the soup brown and defeats the colour.
ingredients: 1 tsp crayfish — no more, or the soup will brown
steps: In a medium pot, cook the beef and ponmo with salt and seasoning cubes for about 15 minutes.
In a clean pot, add 1.5 litres of water. Sieve the garri into the pot and stir over the flame until it is thick. Bring to the boil.
Add the cooked meat with its stock to the garri pot, add the dried pepper and crayfish, and cook about 5 minutes.
Add the periwinkles and smoked fish and allow to boil.

In a mortar, pound some native salt into a powder. Using only a teaspoon's worth, pour it into a clean bowl and add 2 handfuls of starch, 2 cooking spoons of palm oil and a cup of water. Mix together until it flows freely.
Pour the mixture into the cooking pot and blend it in with a wooden spatula until you reach the consistency you want. If it is too thick, add warm water to loosen it.
Simmer a few minutes more, then turn off the heat and leave to cool a few minutes before serving with starch, boiled yam or unripe plantain.
chefTips: A teaspoon of the pounded native salt and no more. It is the emulsifier and it is also an alkali — more is not better and it will taste soapy.
Make the emulsion in a bowl, off the heat, before it goes in. Oil, starch, alkali and water mixed until they flow freely as one thing. That step is what makes owo creamy rather than separated.
One teaspoon of crayfish, because the colour is the dish. The source is explicit: too much crayfish will make your soup brown.
Sieve the garri before it goes in the water. Unsieved, it lumps immediately and never recovers.
Two thickeners, deliberately — garri for body, starch in the emulsion. Most sources use one or the other.
Do not cover the pot. Three independent Delta sources give the same instruction for owo and banga, and it looks like a genuine shared regional technique rather than coincidence.
The finished emulsion should be yellow and thickened. That endpoint is agreed across every source, even though no two agree on how to get there.
commonMistakes: Using more than a teaspoon of native salt.
Adding the palm oil straight to the pot instead of emulsifying it first.
Being generous with the crayfish and browning the soup.
Tipping unsieved garri into the water.
sources: Adapted from 'Ovwoh Soup recipe "Owofibo"', byline 'By Dobby, Updated July 20, 2015', Dobby's Signature. Prep time as printed: 30 minutes. Region as printed: South-south ('Benin' Edo state). Quantities as printed: 7 pieces Beef, 4 pieces Ponmo, 1 small Smoked Fish, 1 cup periwinkles (optional), 1 small Urheri (naive salt), 1 teaspoon of crayfish, 2 cooking spoons Palmoil, 3 handful of yellow garri (sieved), 2 handful of starch, 2 tbsp. Dried pepper, salt to taste, seasoning cubes. The 1.5 litres of water, the teaspoon's worth of pounded native salt and the cup of water for the emulsion are all from the method as printed.

The local-name list is from the page: 'Owo Soup also known as Oghwo/Owho/Owhofibo/Owhoephri/Ogwho-ofigbo is a creamy yellow Niger-delta delicacy, peculiar to the Urhobos, Itsekiris and Isokohs of Delta state, Nigeria.'
THE CRAYFISH CONSTRAINT, as printed on the ingredient line itself: '1 teaspoon of crayfish (using too much crayfish will make your soup brown)'. It is a colour constraint, not a flavour one.

THE EMULSIFICATION STEP, verbatim: 'In a mortar, pound some native salt into powdered form. Using only a teaspoon's worth, pour it into a clean bowl, adding 2 handful of starch, 2 cooking spoons of palm oil and a cup of water. Mix all together until it flows freely.' This is the clearest printed emulsification instruction found in any source consulted.
AUTHOR'S OWN NOTE: 'Although i made mine really thick at first, i had to loosen it up with a little water later on.'

A CLEAN REGIONAL SPLIT, worth recording. Bini and Edo versions of owo USE tomatoes: Guardian Nigeria gives 5 fresh tomatoes or 1 cup tomato puree, and Laura Edet's Edo recipe gives 250 g of fresh tomatoes. Urhobo and Delta versions use NO tomatoes: this recipe and the All Nigerian Recipes Urhobo version both omit them entirely. Two sources each side and no author crosses over.

The same split applies to the thickener: Urhobo and Delta versions thicken with garri — 1 cup in the All Nigerian Recipes version, independently — while the Bini and Edo versions use no thickener at all and rely on the oil-and-alkali emulsion alone for body.

DISAGREEMENT on the alkali quantity, NOT reconciled and worth real caution. Guardian Nigeria's Bini version gives 1/2 teaspoon; All Nigerian Recipes' Urhobo version gives 2 teaspoons; and a third named source, Bawo at withlovebawo.com, gives 2 1/2 to 3 tablespoons dissolved in 6 tablespoons of water for a much larger batch built on 8 cups of water. At roughly 3 teaspoons to the tablespoon that is some fifteen times the Guardian's figure. Batch size explains part of it and not all of it. This is the single most dangerous number in the collection to average, and it is not averaged: the teaspoon's worth specified by this recipe is what is given.

DISAGREEMENT on when the alkali meets the oil — four sources, four sequences. Off-heat before cooking (All Nigerian Recipes, which decants potash water into palm oil in a separate container and stirs 'until the oil turns yellow and thickens'); in the pot, oil first then alkali (Bawo); in the pot, alkali first then oil (Guardian); and off-heat after cooking (Laura Edet, who removes the pot from the heat, cools 10 minutes, then stirs the oil in gradually 'until it is thick in conistency and golden yellow in colour'). The endpoint cue is consistent even where the sequence is not — yellow and thickened.

ON NOT COVERING THE POT: Bawo's owo says 'DO NOT COVER THE SOUP'; All Nigerian Recipes says not to cover at the garri stage, to prevent boiling over; and two Delta banga sources give the same instruction (NGA044, NGA045). Three independent Delta sources, same technique.

GAP: Laura Edet's Edo cookbook, reached only via a corrupted OCR transcription at edoworld.net, is the most promising unexploited Edo source found. Its methods are legible but its numbers are not, so no quantity from it is used here.
storage: 3 days refrigerated. The emulsion may separate and will come back with gentle heat and stirring.
reheating: Low heat, stirring, with warm water to loosen.
healthBenefits: Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
Periwinkle is very lean and high in iron.
culturalNote: Owo is the Delta's creamy yellow soup and it belongs with starch — usi — in the way that gbegiri belongs with amala. The emulsification at its centre is the same piece of knowledge that runs through nkwobi, isi ewu and abacha in the southeast: palm oil plus an alkali plus agitation gives you a thick yellow sauce instead of oil floating on water. Different peoples, different dishes, one technique.
